w: Eighteen- to twenty-foot busts of every U.S. president from Washington to George W. Bush once stood in a ten-acre sculpture park here. When it closed, the concrete heads were hauled to a nearby field and left exposed to the weather, cracking and moldering where they lay. The decay became its own attraction; the site now runs periodic tours of the ruined giants.
s: Giant concrete presidents, abandoned to rot in a field
_facts: 18-20 ft busts of presidents Washington to G.W. Bush
heads moved to a field after the park closed and decayed from exposure
site now offers periodic tours of the decayed heads

w: Twenty-three miles of road link Jamestown, Williamsburg and Yorktown without a billboard, truck or traffic light in sight, built in stages between 1930 and 1957 and screened from commercial view the whole way. It carries the deadpan official designation State Route 90003, but is better known as one of only 31 All-American Roads in the country, running out to the James and York rivers.
s: 23 miles linking Jamestown, Williamsburg and Yorktown
_facts: 23-mile scenic parkway linking Jamestown, Williamsburg and Yorktown
built 1930-1957, part of Colonial National Historical Park
one of 31 All-American Roads in the US

w: The House of Burgesses sat here from 1705, six years after the capital moved up from Jamestown, until Richmond took over in 1780. Fire destroyed the first building in 1747; its replacement lasted until the move. The Capitol standing today is a 1930s reconstruction, part of the original Colonial Williamsburg restoration -- and it has now stood far longer than both original buildings combined.
s: Rebuilt colonial capitol, home to the House of Burgesses
_facts: housed the Virginia General Assembly and House of Burgesses, 1705-1780
reconstructed in the early 1930s as part of Colonial Williamsburg

w: Built in three phases between 1937 and 1972 as John D. Rockefeller Jr.'s vehicle for selling Williamsburg's restoration to influential Americans, this Colonial Revival brick inn has hosted Queen Elizabeth II and Prince Philip twice -- in 1957 and 2007, for the 350th and 400th anniversaries of the Jamestown landing. It has been listed on the National Register of Historic Places since 1997.
s: Rockefeller's showpiece inn, twice host to the Queen
_facts: built 1937-1972, Colonial Revival brick, backed by John D. Rockefeller Jr.
hosted Queen Elizabeth II and Prince Philip in 1957 and 2007
listed on the National Register of Historic Places since 1997

w: When royal governors dissolved the House of Burgesses for defying the Crown, the ousted legislators reconvened at this tavern instead -- one of the largest in colonial Virginia. The Phi Beta Kappa Society was founded in its rooms on December 5, 1776. Rebuilt in 1930-31, it was the first building restored in Colonial Williamsburg, and is kept today as a museum rather than a working tavern.
s: Where ousted legislators met and Phi Beta Kappa began
_facts: gathering place for legislators after royal governors dissolved the House of Burgesses
Phi Beta Kappa Society founded here December 5, 1776
rebuilt 1930-31, first building reconstructed in Colonial Williamsburg
